lateral promise was confined to damages.74 This outcome attracted criticism75 on 
the basis that unilateral promises to contract are fully constituted contracts, from 
which it was argued to follow that they should be specifically enforceable.
The reforms abolished this limitation. According to paragraph 2 of new article 
1124, where a unilateral promise to contract is revoked during the period allowed 
for the beneficiary to exercise their right, thus breaching that contract, this does 
not prevent the formation of the promised contract. The beneficiary can seek spe­
cific enforcement.76 This reinforces the effectiveness and certainty of the unilateral 
promise.77
(iv)  The enforcement of specific enforcement orders
The effectiveness of specific enforcement in France is given considerable assistance 
by a separate, ancillary enforcement mechanism known as the astreinte. This is a 
court order made alongside and in support of an order for the specific enforcement 
of a contractual obligation that requires positive action. It prescribes a period of 
time—​usually in days, weeks, or months—​for each of which the promisor is in de­
fault, they will be liable to pay a monetary penalty to the injured party.
The astreinte is a means of coercing the promisor to comply with a specific en­
forcement order. Whilst the promisor is not physically compelled to perform, in 
that they are at liberty not to comply, that will give rise to a liability to pay an ever 
increasing penalty. This is set at a level that is in proportion to their financial means 
although, in order to be effective, it will generally be greater than the advantage 
that they stand to gain from non-​performance.78 In practice, the resulting pres­
sure is usually effective to bring about performance because the liability will other­
wise quickly become substantial. Failure is rare since no one’s wealth can hold out 
indefinitely.
The nature of the astreinte is unequivocally punitive. It is granted in terrorem
